Helios Towers (HTWS-GB): investment memo · 3 November 2026 · Price 205.2p

Helios Towers: a contracted lease-up compounder priced as a frontier risk, worth buying while the market watches the noisy earnings line instead of the contracted cash line

Written on 3 November 2026, two days before the Q3 2026 trading update on 5 November. Price 205.2p (about 2.75 USD); market value about 2,867 USDm; enterprise value about 4,500 USDm (FactSet); net debt including leases 1,828 USDm (June 2026). Money is in USD millions unless stated. The bases used for EBITDA, EPS and the model are set out in the end notes.

0Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The one-line case. Helios Towers is a lease-up compounder harvesting the tower grid it built in 2020 to 2022. New tenancies on a fixed cost and capital base lift EBITDA by 10 to 13 percent a year with near-contractual certainty, and a fixed finance charge plus a shrinking share count turn that EBITDA growth into EPS that roughly doubles in FY2027 and compounds at 20 to 25 percent a year afterwards. At 8.5x FY2026 EBITDA and the 44th percentile of its own P/E history, the share price reflects a frontier-market discount, not the operating certainty.
+65% / +120%my central total return to December 2027 / June 2029, at my fair multiple of about 20x
+39% / +86%the total return at an unchanged multiple, from earnings and buybacks alone
+117% / +192%the model's return at the guideline multiple of 26.28x, which I treat as a ceiling
145p to 180pthe fair trough at 6.5x to 7.0x forward EBITDA (−12 to −29 percent)

The eight things Richard should hold in mind.

1

Helios Towers is two businesses in one share: a highly predictable tower operator and a leveraged, frontier-taxed equity line. The operating company is as predictable as anything in European infrastructure. It holds 5.9 USDbn of non-cancellable, indexed contracts with 6.5 years remaining and a 1 percent cap on churn, it has beaten EBITDA expectations for fourteen consecutive quarters, and its FY2027 EBITDA is known within about ±4 percent. The equity line is a leveraged residual: FY2027 EPS is known only within about ±30 percent, and the range is skewed downward by two one-sided items that nobody forecasts (non-cash currency losses on intercompany loans, and swings in the tax charge). The case is therefore strongest where it is simplest (EBITDA, recurring cash and distributions) and weakest where the model values it (EPS at a P/E multiple).

2

FY2026 is the peak year for tenancy additions, and FY2027 is the peak year for reported growth. Tenancy additions roughly doubled to about 4,100 in FY2026 (2,538 in FY2025) because three operators front-loaded their 4G capex. A tenancy added in 2026 earns a full year of revenue in 2027, so FY2027 revenue still grows about 10 percent and EBITDA 12.6 percent even as additions fall to about 3,000; reported growth peaks in H1 2027 at about +11 percent. The rate of change has already turned: Q2 2026 additions were below Q1, and guidance implies H2 2026 at roughly half the H1 run-rate. The market will see the first sequential fall on 5 November.

3

Management sets guidance below the run-rate, so guidance is likely to be raised or tightened upward at most of the next six reporting events (a 60 to 70 percent probability at each). About 25 to 30 USDm of FY2027 EBITDA is already contracted carry from the tenancies added in H1 2026, and management under-promises by habit. FY2027 EBITDA guidance in March 2027 will probably open at 585 to 600 USDm, against consensus of 594 USDm and the model's 598 USDm, and then be raised.

4

The sequencing of news is the main problem for the share price: the unfavourable surprises arrive first. A sequential fall in additions comes on 5 November 2026. A FY2026 EPS print about a quarter below consensus comes in March 2027 (the model's 0.07 USD against consensus of 0.09 USD), because H1 2026 finance costs of 125.8 USDm and a 45.6 percent interim tax rate are already in the books. The favourable surprises mature later, through 2027 and 2028: FY2027 guidance at or above consensus; the effect of the buyback on the share count, which brokers have not modelled; early delivery and a refresh of the IMPACT 2030 targets; and a step-up in distributions as leverage falls through 3.0x.

5

Consensus is right on revenue and EBITDA and wrong on EPS: too high for FY2026 and too low for FY2027 to FY2029. Revenue and EBITDA consensus sit within 1 percent of the model in every year to FY2028. FY2026 EPS consensus (0.090 USD) is about 25 to 40 percent too high. FY2027 to FY2029 EPS consensus (0.130, 0.170 and 0.200 USD) is 2 to 9 percent too low on a diluted basis, because brokers hold the share count flat while 175 USDm of buybacks retire about 5 percent of the shares by end-2027.

6

Beyond eighteen months, the largest fundamental risk is concentrated in one market, two counterparties and a known date: the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) lease renewals of 2028 to 2029. The company's own schedule of contracted revenue shows contracted revenue in Central and Southern Africa falling by 68 USDm (15 percent) from 2027 to 2029, as Airtel Africa's and Orange's master leases in the DRC reach their initial terms; Oman's contracts run past 2030. Every emerging-market precedent ended with the tower company trading a modest concession for ten more years of term. The model deducts a concession of about 1 percent of group revenue, and I put the probability of a material concession (3 to 5 percent of revenue) at 25 to 30 percent over three years. No broker models any of these renewals.

7

The downside sits in the valuation multiple, not in the earnings. Debt is about 40 percent of enterprise value, so one turn of EV/EBITDA moves the market value by about 20 percent. A fair trough multiple of 6.5x to 7.0x forward EBITDA gives 145p to 180p (−12 to −29 percent); the 6x private-market reference (MTN is paying about 6x EBITDA for IHS) gives about −45 percent. Each year of 10 percent EBITDA growth lifts the trough price by 15 to 20 percent, so time works for the holder.

8

The model's return depends more on a higher multiple than on earnings growth, and I would not rely on the higher multiple. At the guideline fair multiple of 26.28x two-year-forward earnings, the model returns +117 percent to December 2027 and +192 percent to June 2029, and the re-rating contributes +57 percentage points of the first figure. The 26.28x is the 60th percentile of a ten-year P/E history generated by a loss-making company. The market values Helios on EV/EBITDA and recurring free cash flow, and the frontier discount stays "locked" while emerging-market sentiment and interest rates are adverse. My fair multiple is about 20x (about 9.5x forward EBITDA). At 20x, the return is about +65 percent to December 2027 and about +120 percent to June 2029, four fifths of it from earnings. At an unchanged multiple, the return is still about +39 percent and +86 percent.

The setup. Helios Towers is a "Demand-driven EPSU" setup (an EPS upgrade driven by customer demand): three operators' 4G capex cycle steps up tenancies and EBITDA, and fixed interest costs and buybacks carry that step-up into EPS. A mechanical programme of deleveraging and buybacks adds a kicker. The case does not depend on a cause for concern clearing, although two small concerns (the overhang of pre-IPO shareholders and the satellite scare) are clearing in the background.

What I would do with the dated events

5 November 2026 tests volume. Q3 additions above 900 mean a guidance raise; 700 to 900 mean a hold; below 600 widens the range of outcomes for FY2027.

March 2027 brings the most information and the greatest optical risk. It combines the FY2026 EPS miss, the FY2027 guidance, the redemption of the convertible bond and the tax reconciliation.

H2 2027 is when the narrative must shift from "growth" to "cash per share", or the shares will stall.

1Tailwinds in the operating environment; headwinds and risks

ConclusionThe demand tailwinds are strong, broad and partly front-loaded, while the headwinds bear on the share's multiple and the lines below EBITDA rather than on the business. The operating environment is a clear net positive for the operating forecasts and a mixed influence on the share price over six months.

The structural tailwind: Africa's data runs on wireless, and coverage is still low. Wireless networks carry about 75 percent of African data traffic, against 15 percent in Europe. Mobile coverage reaches 35 percent of the DRC's population and 45 percent of Tanzania's, and smartphone penetration is expected to rise from about 50 percent to over 80 percent by 2030. Management sizes the organic opportunity at 72,000 further tenancies by 2040, roughly double today's 34,455.

The cyclical tailwind: four large operators are spending heavily in 2026. Airtel Africa's cash capex was 389 USDm in its June 2026 quarter against 121 USDm a year earlier, with 1.1 USDbn guided for its year to March 2027. Vodacom targets capex at 13.0 to 14.5 percent of revenue and prioritises Tanzania and the DRC, where its subscribers grew 16 and 11 percent. Orange's Middle East and Africa capex runs at about 1.6 EURbn a year. Omantel's 5G build and 3G retirement produced 454 Helios additions in Oman in H1 2026. Together, the top four African operators raised their capex guidance by about a third.

Helios's own additions show the cycle. Organic tenancy additions were 1,406 in Q1 2026 and 1,105 in Q2 (against consensus of 487 for Q2). The H1 2026 total of 2,511 nearly equalled the 2,538 added in the whole of FY2025.

The caveat is in the customers' own words: part of the 2026 demand is borrowed from 2027 and 2028. Airtel calls its spending "a deliberate frontloading strategy", and its unchanged full-year guidance implies about 220 USDm of capex a quarter in its second half, a third below the first half. Precedents point the same way: US 5G capex peaked in 2022 and normalised within two years, and Indian operators' capex fell from 927 to 596 INRbn between FY2024 and FY2026.

The headwinds act on the multiple and below EBITDA, not on the operating lines. There are six.

  1. Interest rates and the bond-proxy trade. The US 10-year yield is near 5.1 percent, towers are described as "the pure long-duration bond proxy", and the portfolio's sector stance on towers is Underweight. The effect on Helios is weak, because its six-month correlation with the European tower basket is only 0.27 (R-squared 8 percent).
  2. Frontier-market risk appetite. Ghana's reserves are under pressure and the cedi has fallen 12 percent in nine months; Senegal is rated Caa1; Coface has downgraded Tanzania. Morgan Stanley says the stock "trades in line with higher-risk African equities" and that its discount is "locked" until emerging-market sentiment shifts.
  3. Sovereign and regulatory risk. About 104 to 106 USDm of tax assessments are unprovided. The Banque Centrale du Congo bans physical foreign-currency cash from 9 April 2027; the ban is probably benign for Helios because its collections are electronic and billed in dollars, but it signals de-dollarisation in the company's largest market.
  4. Tower options controlled by customers. Esengo Towers (Vodacom and Orange) plans 1,000 rural solar sites in the DRC over four years; Eastcastle is growing to 1,800 DRC sites; Bharti's Indus Towers is entering Africa anchored on Airtel; MTN is re-integrating IHS.
  5. Energy. With Brent near 111 USD, higher power costs pass through at nil EBITDA and dilute the margin percentage by 0.5 to 0.7 points.
  6. Satellites, a fading headwind. Direct-to-cell satellite service carried 0.0003 percent of T-Mobile's traffic, and Airtel has signed SpaceX as a complement to towers, not a substitute.

Inference: the business and the share are being pulled in opposite directions. The forces that drive revenue and EBITDA are as favourable as at any time since the 2019 IPO. They are broad (three operators, not one project) and visible in customers' cash spending, but part of the demand is borrowed from 2027 to 2028. The forces that act on the equity (the discount rate, frontier-market sentiment, tax and repatriation of cash) are unfavourable, and they act on the multiple and the lines below EBITDA, not on the operating lines.

So what: forecast the operating lines on the tailwind, and carry the headwinds in the tax rate, the finance charge and the multiple. I expect additions to normalise toward 2,000 to 2,500 a year from FY2028, and I treat anything above 3,000 additions in FY2027 as upside.

Counter-case. Jefferies reads the operators' capex as "a more prolonged investment cycle" rather than a pull-forward, and management speaks of a renewed five-year operator cycle. If that reading is right, FY2027 additions stay above 3,500 and FY2028 does not decelerate. The frontier headwind could also reverse: a fall in US yields or an emerging-market rally would lift the multiple without any change in the business.

What would change my view

Airtel Africa's December-quarter capex (reported early in 2027) above about 330 USDm would make me lift FY2027 additions toward 3,500; below about 200 USDm would make me cut them toward 2,000.

A widening of the DRC cash rule to electronic dollar settlement would move repatriation risk from a tail risk to a base-case risk.

Where I differ from the market

The sell-side knows the front-loading debate and is split on it. I sit in the middle, with additions of 4,100, 3,000 and 2,400 for FY2026 to FY2028.

The market has not yet articulated that the growth peak falls in H1 2027 and the first reported deceleration in H2 2027; that timing is my own call.

Score: 72, set by the Rater. Broad, funded external demand reaches nearly all sales: three operators' guided 4G capex (Airtel cash capex 389 vs 121 USDm, top four raising capex by about a third) on top of a structural African data curve (wireless 75% of data, coverage 35-45%, smartphones 50% to 80%+), adding about 10-11% revenue growth in FY2026-27 and a rising margin; it is trimmed by front-loading (Airtel's H2 a third lower, growth back to 5-6% from FY2028), customer-aligned tower ventures (Esengo, Indus, Eastcastle) and FX/power-margin drag. I score above the 63 External change forces group because rates, frontier sentiment and tax act on the multiple and below EBITDA, which belong to topic 9, not on organic revenue and margins; just below RELX's steady structural demand, above Spie's mixed picture.

2Internally-driven corporate change forces; problems and risks

ConclusionA proven, unchanged team is executing a strong, fully funded change on one axis: capital allocation and shareholder returns. A cluster of small governance and earnings-quality negatives in 2026 affects how the company looks, not how its engine works.

The change is a turn in capital allocation, from building the platform to harvesting it. The IMPACT 2030 plan (November 2025) replaced acquisition-led expansion (381 USDm of acquisitions in 2021 to 2022, with leverage peaking at 5.1x) with organic lease-up and distributions. The plan commits over 500 USDm of growth capex to 2030, gated at incremental returns on invested capital (ROIC) of 20 to 35 percent; at least 400 USDm of distributions; and a leverage corridor of 2.5x to 3.5x net debt to EBITDA.

In 2026 the company resourced and accelerated the turn.

  • Guidance: FY2026 tenancy guidance raised from 2,000 to 2,500 to 3,500 to 4,000 (+67 percent on the opening midpoint), and EBITDA guidance from 510 to 525 USDm to 520 to 535 USDm; discretionary capex guidance raised twice, to 215 to 245 USDm.
  • Distributions: a 75 USDm buyback raised to 175 USDm and extended to December 2027 (about 6 percent of market value; about 117 USDm still to spend at July 2026); an inaugural dividend of 25 USDm for FY2026, guided to grow over 10 percent a year.
  • Balance sheet: 500 USDm of 6.75 percent notes due 2031 replaced the 2028 term loan and cut the cost of debt by 40 basis points; an undrawn 250 USDm facility pre-funds the March 2027 convertible bond; 120 USDm of the convertible was tendered below par; Moody's upgraded the company to Ba3, and S&P and Fitch to BB-.
  • Operating standards: build time cut from 167 to 102 days; colocations delivered in under 24 hours; power uptime of 99.99 percent; hybrid power sites up from 29 to 56 percent of the estate; group ROIC up from 10.3 percent (2022) to 14.4 percent (H1 2026).

The negatives are real but small, and mostly concern optics and earnings quality. Seven stand out.

  • The company stopped disclosing adjusted gross margin just as the pass-through of power costs began to dilute the margin percentage, and it restated segment EBITDA in Q1 2026.
  • Maximum bonus and long-term incentive plan awards were raised (from 175 to 200 percent and from 200 to 250 percent of salary), with a proposal to drop the 5 percent cap on discretionary share plans.
  • The chief executive sold 24 percent of his stake in March 2026.
  • Only 50 percent of the board is independent.
  • Related-party receivables of 50.1 USDm are unsecured and interest-free, and the research does not explain them.
  • Unrecognised potential contract revenue rose 149 percent to 46.8 USDm (a key audit matter); my tripwire is 55 USDm.
  • The 2024 extension of tower lives from 15 to 30 years cut depreciation by 52.8 USDm a year and produced the company's first positive net income.

Inference: the pivot's strength is its funding, and its weakness is its narrowness. Every element of the pivot is funded from recurring free cash flow (220 to 235 USDm guided for FY2026), and none from new debt. But there is no change in leadership, perimeter, pricing or cost structure to broaden it. The 2030 targets, set before the demand surge, are already stale: the target of over 42,000 tenancies needs only about 1,400 additions a year from end-2026, against a path of 2,300 to 3,000.

So what: capital allocation is predictable. I expect capex at the top of guidance while demand is strong, the buyback finishing in 2027, a dividend growing over 10 percent a year, and leverage drifting to about 3.3x at end-2026 (not the 3.0x that an old broker marker implied) and about 3.0x at end-2027, through EBITDA growth rather than debt repayment. The next internal step is a refresh of the 2030 targets with a larger distribution programme; the model assumes new buybacks of 110, 150 and 180 USDm in FY2028 to FY2030.

Counter-case. The 2026 governance cluster could mark the start of a looser public company. The sponsors' exit removed the last shareholder-nominated director, the related-party receivables are unexplained, and the withdrawn margin measure was the one that would have shown the dilution from power pass-through. A 400 USDm "flexible capital" line in IMPACT 2030 is where an acquisition misstep would come from.

What would change my view

Any acquisition outside the nine existing markets; a buyback paused to fund capex; unrecognised contract revenue above 55 USDm; any further withdrawal of disclosure.

Where I differ from the market

Every broker covers the pivot fully and positively, and all of them ignore the governance cluster. I weight the cluster as the reason the equity line has traded weaker than the operating line, not as a change to the business's mechanism.

Score: 64, set by the Rater. A funded, well-executed pivot from acquisition-led growth to organic lease-up and distributions (175 USDm buyback, about 6% of market value; inaugural dividend; refinancing at lower cost; rating upgrades) with measurable rising standards (build time 167 to 102 days, hybrid sites 29% to 56%, ROIC 10.3% to 14.4%) adds about 5% to EPS by 2027 through the share count plus cheaper debt, but it is narrow (no perimeter, pricing or cost-structure change) and dented by small governance and earnings-quality negatives (CEO sale, bonus caps raised, unexplained related-party receivables, a withdrawn margin disclosure). In line with the 62 group; just below Redcare's operating-leverage pivot, above Teqnion's recovery.

3Value chain and industry structure; business model and barriers; financial profile; management

ConclusionHelios has a favourable, concentrated and rational industry structure; a strong, self-reinforcing but defensive moat; a financial profile that is best in its sector on growth and leverage and in the bottom quartile on margin and earnings quality; and a delivery-focused management whose one untested skill is renegotiating with customers who now hold alternatives.

Industry structure: as favourable as tower markets get, with the fragility on the customer side rather than among rivals. Helios is the largest independent tower company in seven of its nine markets. It owns 60 percent of marketable towers in Tanzania and 42 percent of all towers (75 percent of independent towers) in the DRC, and it is the sole independent in Madagascar and Malawi. Its competitors put margins first and build only against ten-year anchor contracts: IHS is being bought by MTN, American Tower is prioritising developed markets, and SBA builds selectively. The barriers to entry are high: 100k to 150k USD per tower, plus permits, aviation and environmental clearances, and the power logistics of delivering 99.99 percent uptime where the grid supplies power for only eight to seventeen hours a day.

The structure bends on the customer side. The top four customers provide 72 percent of revenue (Airtel 28 percent, Vodacom 23, Orange 11, Axian 10) and over 90 percent of receivables, with no collateral. Those same customers are acquiring tower options of their own: Esengo, Eastcastle's financed growth, Indus Towers with Bharti, and MTN with IHS. None of these options touches existing tenancies, but together they cap long-run pricing power and strengthen the customers' hand at renewal.

Business model and moat: five advantages, of which two are decisive.

  • Contracts and switching costs (decisive). Master leases run ten to fifteen years, are non-cancellable and are all-or-nothing at renewal; churn is capped at 1 percent; the remaining contract value is payable on early exit; and moving a customer's active equipment costs about 50k EUR per site.
  • Power management and site density (decisive). Power uptime is 99.99 percent, against an African norm of 95 to 98 percent. Each colocation raises a site's cash-on-cash return (about 12 percent with one tenant, about 25 percent with two, over 30 percent with three) and strengthens the incumbent's claim on the next tenant; tenancies and EBITDA have moved with a correlation of 0.96.
  • The revealed-preference test. Customers pay about 30 percent less than the cost of building their own towers, and they keep adding tenancies at record rates.

The moat's limit is that it is defensive. Indexation has held through hyperinflation and devaluations, but there is no evidence of real price rises, and the contractual protection comes up for renegotiation in the DRC in 2028 to 2029.

Financial profile: above the sector average where it matters, and below it where it shows. The EBITDA margin of 55 percent is the sector's lowest (Cellnex 83 percent, Inwit 91, Rai Way 67) because power is a large pass-through cost, not because of weak execution; the margin rises about a point a year on fixed site costs, toward 60 percent by FY2030. EBITDA growth of 11 to 13 percent compares with about 5 percent for European towers. Net debt is 3.4x EBITDA on the company's measure (3.7x on FactSet's, which includes leases), fixed-rate to 2029 and 2031, against 6x to 7x at Cellnex, Inwit and SBA. Free cash flow after all capex and leases is negative in FY2026 because of the capex surge, and then rises to about 200 USDm or more a year by FY2029 (the path is in section 6).

The return on capital is the profile's subtle point: the group earns about its cost of capital today, so the equity case rests on high incremental returns continuing. Reported group ROIC is 14.4 percent against an 11 percent weighted average cost of capital (WACC), but my rough post-tax measure is about 10 percent. Incremental returns are high: about 20 percent pre-tax on the 2026 build mix, and over 100 percent on pure colocations. The weak points sit below EBITDA: a reported tax rate of 71 percent in FY2025, non-cash currency swings, and depreciation flattered by the 2024 extension of tower lives.

Management: a proven operating team whose goals fit this stage of the company. The team has delivered ten consecutive years of EBITDA growth through Ghana's default and the 2022 to 2023 rate shock. It has met or beaten guidance every year, and it raised guidance midpoints in each of 2023, 2024 and 2025 and twice in 2026. Its operating standards are outliers. Every employee is a shareholder, and the long-term incentive plan pays on recurring free cash flow per share and ROIC. The chief executive (sixteen years at the company, CEO since 2022) has run the capital raising, the operations and now the harvest.

The management record has two blemishes and one gap. The first blemish is the acquisition chapter the CEO co-led: the new markets earn about 8.5 percent ROIC against 17.6 percent in established ones. The second is the 2026 alignment wobbles. The goals are stretching on organic growth and deliberately unambitious on expansion, which is right for this stage. The gap is that management has stated no answer to the customer-controlled tower ventures; a hosting or partnership role in Esengo would be the smart response, and nobody has suggested one.

Counter-case. The industry structure is only as strong as the next renewal. If Airtel used Indus Towers' entry into Africa as a credible alternative for new builds, or Esengo moved from rural to suburban sites, the bargaining balance in the DRC would shift, and the most likely renewal outcome would move from a concession traded for term toward a real price cut.

What would change my view

A disclosed DRC renewal on unchanged economics would raise my view of the moat from strong but defensive to strong. A credible move by Indus Towers or Esengo into Helios's suburban sites would lower it.

Where I differ from the market

The sell-side describes the moat and the management well, and asks about the renewals without modelling them. The location of the renewals (the DRC, not Oman) and their concentration (two counterparties) come from the company's own contracted-revenue schedule, and nobody discusses them. I also weight the post-tax group return (about equal to WACC) more heavily than the headline 14.4 percent.

Score: 68, set by the Rater. A concentrated, rational, barrier-protected tower structure (number one independent in seven of nine markets, non-cancellable indexed leases, 1% churn cap, density loops, uptime 99.99%) and a proven management team, with very high operating predictability and new capital earning about 20% pre-tax (over 100% on colocations); against that, a defensive moat with no real pricing power, 72% customer concentration facing DRC renewals in 2028-29, a frontier sovereign layer and post-tax group returns only about at the 11% WACC. The 2% ROIC (17th percentile) understates quality through goodwill, tax and FX, while the 90th-percentile EBITDA margin overstates nothing; coherent with the groups (74, 68, 46, 66), just below Tele2's rational oligopoly with cleaner returns, above Carlsberg.

4Conservative guidance; keeping the sell-side conservative; the track record of delivery and upgrades

ConclusionHelios has a textbook record of under-promising and delivering on every operating line: guidance is a floor, and sell-side operating estimates sit on that floor. The conservatism stops at EBITDA. Below EBITDA the company guides nothing, the sell-side has to guess, and it has guessed too high.

Current guidance is set well below the run-rate. The FY2026 guidance set in July implies 495 to 745 additions a quarter in H2 2026, against 1,255 a quarter delivered in H1. The EBITDA midpoint implies H2 growth of about 10 percent, against 14 percent in H1, even though management describes a pipeline giving "solid volume visibility into fiscal year 2027".

The pattern is long-standing. FY2023 additions came in 31 percent above the top of the opening range; the target tenancy ratio of 2.2x was reached a year early; FY2025 EBITDA was 471.1 USDm against 470 USDm guided. The shape of the 2026 raises (volume +67 percent, EBITDA +2 percent, capex +35 USDm) is the shape of a management that raises only what it already has in hand.

Below EBITDA, the company guides nothing, and it signals that it wants to be valued on cash. There is no guidance for the tax rate, the finance charge, currency or EPS. The company's own per-share measures are diluted Adjusted EBITDA per share and recurring free cash flow per share, the clearest possible signal that it intends to be valued on cash and EBITDA. Consensus sits on top of the operating guidance (FY2026 EBITDA consensus of 528 USDm against a guidance midpoint of 527.5 USDm; the four brokers' FY2027 EBITDA within 3 percent of each other) and far above where the EPS line will land.

The IMPACT 2030 targets are already beaten on current trajectories, except for the EBITDA growth target. The EBITDA target (a compound annual growth rate of over 9 percent) is the one that the 2026 surge makes harder: measured from the inflated FY2026 base, it comes out at about 8.8 percent. Management will present it as met, measured from 2025.

Inference: guidance is a floor built from a run-rate already in hand, and in this business a volume raise in one year becomes a guidance raise in the next. Every 500 tenancies add over 10 USDm of annualised EBITDA, so 2026's additions are 2027's upgrades. The record of EPS consensus is the opposite of the operating record. FY2025 EPS consensus fell 52 percent in the twelve months before the results, and FY2026 EPS consensus has fallen 19 percent in the last twelve months and has more than halved overall, from 0.238 USD to 0.089 USD. The cause has always been tax, currency or finance costs, never EBITDA.

So what: build the operating model above the guidance midpoints, and build the EPS bridge independently of the company. I expect the FY2027 EBITDA guidance in March 2027 to open at 585 to 600 USDm, and the FY2027 additions guidance at 2,000 to 2,500 or 2,500 to 3,000. The additions range will read as a deceleration even though it is conservative. I put the probability of a partial refresh of the 2030 targets (tenancies, cash and distributions) by March 2028 at about 60 percent, with the EBITDA growth target held.

Counter-case. Conservatism is now the consensus description of the company, so beats are expected and have not been rewarded: the shares fell about 23 percent from the June high through the July beat-and-raise, a fall attributed to selling by pre-IPO holders that is now largely done. A stock that every analyst rates a Buy has no rating upgrades left: all four brokers rate it a Buy, and I put the probability of a first Hold within eighteen months at about 30 percent. New Street, with the lowest target, is the likeliest candidate, most plausibly after the FY2026 EPS print.

What would change my view

A guidance cut at any of the six events (joint probability about 10 to 15 percent, concentrated in H2 2027 and in the cash line rather than EBITDA); a FY2027 opening EBITDA range below 580 USDm; an IMPACT 2030 refresh that raised the EBITDA growth target, which would tell me that management sees the operator cycle as prolonged.

Where I differ from the market

On the pattern, I agree with every broker. On the figures, my FY2026 EBITDA (531 USDm) is at the top of the guidance range, my additions (4,100) are above it, and my FY2027 EBITDA (598 USDm) is above where guidance will open. On EPS, the market is about to learn that "conservative guidance" says nothing about the lines that decide the EPS print.

Score: 80, set by the Rater. A textbook operating record: guidance met or beaten every year, midpoints raised in 2023, 2024, 2025 and twice in 2026, fourteen consecutive quarterly EBITDA beats, FY2023 additions 31% above the top of the range, IMPACT targets reached early, and current H2 2026 guidance set at roughly half the H1 run-rate, so the conservatism is current. Held below AQ because the record against EPS consensus is poor (FY2025 EPS consensus fell 52% before the print, FY2026 down 19%, another miss due in March 2027): nothing is guided below EBITDA, and that absence is not itself negative, but the sell-side has been cut every year on that line; coherent with Guidance 78 and Sell-side estimates 44.

5Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost-out and feedback loops: why revenue growth becomes outsized profit growth

ConclusionHelios has a near-ideal leverage structure on the way up: fixed site costs, fixed interest, a tax charge fixed in dollars and a shrinking share count turn 7 to 12 percent EBITDA growth into 20 to 100 percent EPS growth. Pricing power is defensive only, and the cost-out lever is modest. The same gearing works in reverse on the two lines that nobody controls: currency and tax.

Operating leverage: about half of the cash cost base is fixed, so a new colocation earns about 80 percent at the margin. Of about 420 USDm of annual cash operating cost, about 200 USDm is power passed through to customers at nil margin, and about 215 USDm (site costs of about 100 USDm and overheads of about 117 USDm) is genuinely fixed. Hence the incremental EBITDA margin on a colocation is about 80 percent, against a 55 percent group margin; in FY2025 revenue grew 7.8 percent while cost of sales grew 1.3 percent. Below EBITDA, depreciation grows only 4 to 5 percent a year (towers are now on 30-year lives), so operating profit grows about 18 percent in each of FY2026 and FY2027 on EBITDA growth of 12.7 percent.

Financial leverage: a fixed finance charge, a dollar tax charge and buybacks amplify the operating leverage.

  • Finance charge. The charge is fixed at about 180 USDm a year (over 90 percent of debt is fixed-rate; a 100 basis point rise in rates costs about 2.7 USDm). Operating profit rises from about 293 USDm (FY2025) to about 531 USDm (FY2030), so pre-tax profit rises 2.7 times.
  • Tax charge. The tax charge in dollars is driven by the operating companies' profits (cash tax is guided at 5 to 6 percent of revenue), so the tax rate on group pre-tax profit falls mechanically, from about 48 percent in FY2026 (including minorities) to about 33 percent.
  • Share count. Buybacks of 52, 99, 110, 150 and 180 USDm cut the share count by about 15 percent by FY2030.

The arithmetic of the gearing: every dollar of revenue growth is multiplied about three times on the way to EPS. The model's EPS rises 55 percent, from 0.14 USD (FY2027) to 0.22 USD (FY2029). The rise decomposes multiplicatively into five factors: EBITDA (+16 percent); operating leverage, measured as EBITA over EBITDA, rising from 0.68 to 0.70 (+3 percent); financial leverage, measured as pre-tax profit over EBITA, rising from 0.56 to 0.64 (+14 percent); the tax ratio, measured as net income over pre-tax profit, rising from 0.62 to 0.66 (+6 percent); and the falling share count (+7 percent).

The multiplier works identically in reverse, and it fades over time. A change of 1,000 tenancies is 3.4 percent of FY2027 EBITDA and about 9 percent of FY2027 EPS. The gearing is highest in FY2027, when EPS roughly doubles on EBITDA growth of 12.6 percent, and it falls each year as interest shrinks relative to operating profit; by FY2029, EPS grows about 23 percent on EBITDA growth of about 7 percent.

Pricing power is defensive only, and the business leans more on indexation just as the DRC renewals test it. Uncapped annual inflation escalators (linked to US CPI on the 69 percent of revenue in dollars or dollar-pegged currencies) and power escalators with floors added about 43 USDm of revenue in FY2025 and offset 28 USDm of currency drag. Price contributes about 2 to 2.5 points of revenue growth and about 0.4 points of margin a year. Price is about a quarter of revenue growth in FY2026 and FY2027 and 35 to 40 percent of it in FY2028 to FY2030. There is no offensive pricing power, and the latent direction of price at renewal is down.

Cost-out is small on the profit and loss account and large on cash. Power efficiency adds about 4 to 5 USDm of EBITDA a year, and overhead leverage adds about 1.5 points of margin by FY2030; cutting security or maintenance would damage the uptime that is the product. On cash, discretionary capex falls from about 230 USDm in FY2026 to about 115 to 120 USDm a year from FY2028, which swings free cash flow by about 110 USDm.

Feedback loops: the two reinforcing loops dominate FY2027; the three balancing loops set the growth rate from FY2028 but not the level of revenue, because the installed base is contracted. The reinforcing loops are density (each tenant raises site returns, switching costs and the odds of the next colocation) and cash return (falling leverage releases buybacks, which raise cash per share, which improves credit ratings and the cost of debt). The balancing loops are the front-loading of operator capex; capex funding, which delays cash while demand is strong and releases it afterwards; and customer cost, in which a rising tower bill pushes operators toward joint builds and renewal pressure.

Counter-case. Leverage of this kind also amplifies the misses. A currency loss of the FY2023 size (86 USDm) would take more than half of FY2027 net income. A 10 percent adverse move across the non-pegged currencies costs about 14 USDm of EBITDA. The margin percentage is hostage to the oil price, even though EBITDA in dollars is not.

What would change my view

Evidence of real price increases at renewal would add an offensive lever. A rise in the share of amendments within additions would lower revenue per incremental tenancy below the 27.7k USD I assume, because amendments earn less than full colocations.

Where I differ from the market

The sell-side understands the operating leverage completely and the financial leverage inconsistently: it models the falling tax rate as a residual rather than a mechanism, and most brokers hold the share count flat. I treat the share count as the most reliable EPS lever after EBITDA, and the tax rate's direction as reliable but its level as noisy.

Score: 80, set by the Rater. Several gears are proven and work together: about 215 USDm of a 420 USDm cash cost base is fixed and power is a nil-margin pass-through, so a colocation carries about 80% incremental EBITDA margin; a fixed 180 USDm finance charge, a dollar tax charge and buybacks cutting the share count about 15% turn FY2027-29 EBITDA growth of 16% into EPS growth of 55%, about three times; density and cash-return loops reinforce. Held below 90 because pricing is indexation-only with no real price rises and a latent downward direction at the DRC renewals, cost-out is small, and the 3.4-3.8x leverage and FX on intercompany loans make the same gearing bite on the downside.

6Forecast financials; scope for double-digit growth; scope for higher growth and margins than the past

ConclusionThe forecasts are tightly anchored at the EBITDA and recurring-cash level: double-digit growth for two more years, then 7 to 9 percent, on a margin rising to 60 percent, and far better in quality than the acquisition-led past. They are loosely anchored at the EPS level, where the model is well below consensus for FY2026 and modestly above it for FY2027 to FY2029, and where I carry the currency line as a stated risk rather than as a forecast input.

The forecasts of record (model update 2). The table sets out each line; my view of each line follows it.

The model's own equity free cash flow (-106, 58, 129, 172 and 201 USDm for FY2026 to FY2030) is lower than the cash figures above by the non-cash content of the finance and tax lines; the difference does not affect the return, which is struck on EPS. Consensus revenue and EBITDA are within 1 percent of the model in every year to FY2028.

Why these forecasts and not others: each line rests on one stated mechanism.

  • Revenue is a volume forecast. Revenue is tenancies multiplied by a flat 27.7k USD per average tenancy, because escalators are offset by mix and currency. The FY2026 figure of 4,100 additions assumes Q3 and Q4 above the 495 to 745 a quarter that guidance implies, based on the company's record of beating company-compiled tenancy consensus by 127 to 150 percent in each quarter of 2026. The FY2027 figure of 3,000 is a 27 percent fall, consistent with Airtel's own capex phasing. The figure of 2,300 a year afterwards matches management's informal guide of "about 6 percent a year".
  • The margin rises about a point a year from the mechanics described in section 5, less about 0.5 points for build dilution and a modest DRC renewal concession in FY2028 to FY2029.
  • The finance line takes the H1 2026 actual (125.8 USDm of finance costs, or about 101 USDm net before the 21.8 USDm currency loss), adds a clean second half, and then runs at about 180 USDm a year, with the convertible bond refinanced at about 7.5 to 8 percent and the 7.5 percent notes due 2029 refinanced more cheaply.
  • The tax line preserves the dollar tax charge (cash tax of 6 to 8 percent of revenue, slightly above the guided 5 to 6 percent, plus deferred tax) on the lower pre-tax profit, because the debt sits in holding companies whose losses cannot be relieved against operating profits.

I leave the model's inputs unchanged: I considered two changes and rejected both.

  1. An expected currency loss on intercompany loans of about 10 to 15 USDm a year from FY2027. The case for including it is that frontier currencies fall more often than they rise, and the 2025 designation of some intercompany loans as net investments (which keeps their currency moves out of the income statement) is only partial, as the H1 2026 loss shows. I keep zero because the fair multiple in section 11 is drawn from a P/E history built on consensus EPS, which excludes the item; putting the loss into the base would mismatch the earnings and the multiple. I carry the item instead as the largest single risk to every year's EPS, with its expected value stated in section 9.
  2. Lifting FY2027 additions toward 3,500, on Jefferies's "prolonged cycle" reading. I keep 3,000 because Airtel's own guidance implies a third less capex in its second half, and the Q3 update on 5 November will give better evidence than I have today.

Growth is double-digit for two years at every line, and the quality of growth is far better than in the past. Revenue growth is double-digit in FY2026 and FY2027 and mid-single-digit afterwards; EBITDA growth is double-digit for two years and 7 to 9 percent afterwards; EPS growth is double-digit or far higher in every year to FY2030. Every line below revenue grows faster than revenue: the ratio of growth to revenue growth is about 1.2 for EBITDA, about 1.6 for operating profit and about 6 for net income.

The past six years were faster but bought; the next five are slower but organic. From FY2019 to FY2025, revenue grew 14 percent a year, but about half of that growth was acquired, at about 6 percent ROIC, and funded to 5.1x leverage; the margin rose 10 points, mostly as acquired portfolios leased up. From FY2025 to FY2030, revenue grows 7.8 percent a year, all of it organic, at incremental returns of 20 to 100 percent; free cash flow turns positive permanently, and the share count falls 3.5 percent a year instead of rising.

The range of outcomes for FY2027 is narrow for EBITDA and wide for net income, and FY2026 EPS is the most likely miss in the case.

578 to 618 USDmFY2027 EBITDA around 598. Contracted carry locks the floor; ±1,000 additions is ±10 USDm in the year; fuel and currency ±8 USDm
100 to 170 USDmFY2027 net income around 142, skewed down: volume ±13, tax ±11, finance ±6, currency 0 to −40
0.060 to 0.085 USDFY2026 diluted EPS, against consensus of 0.090 USD

Scenarios for FY2030: the downside costs about a quarter of EPS but little free cash flow, because capex falls with demand. In the upside scenario (about 20 percent probability), the operator cycle runs five years, additions hold near 3,000 and renewals are clean; FY2030 EBITDA is about 790 to 800 USDm and EPS about 0.31 USD. In the downside scenario (about 25 percent), additions fall to about 1,500 a year from FY2028, the DRC concession is material and currency drag persists; FY2030 EBITDA is about 650 to 670 USDm and EPS about 0.20 to 0.22 USD, with free cash flow still about 200 USDm. A restriction on repatriating cash from the DRC or Tanzania (5 to 10 percent probability) sits outside both scenarios as a tail risk that stops distributions rather than earnings.

What would change my view

Q3 additions below 600 (I would cut FY2027 additions toward 2,500); a FY2026 tax charge above about 80 USDm or a currency loss in the second half (I would lower FY2027 EPS); FY2027 opening EBITDA guidance above 600 USDm (I would lift the volume path).

Where I differ from the market

Operating lines: no difference worth the name. FY2026 EPS: consensus of 0.090 USD is about 25 to 40 percent too high and will be cut at or before March 2027. FY2027 to FY2029 EPS: consensus is 2 to 9 percent too low because it ignores the buyback. Capex: consensus (168 and 160 USDm) assumes the build halves in FY2027; I expect about 200 USDm, because the pipeline and the 150 USDm Senegal commitment carry over, so consensus free cash flow is 20 to 30 USDm too high in FY2027 and FY2028.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. Above 35% gives C: the rate is very high because a thin FY2025-26 EPS residual doubles in FY2027 on contracted carry, fixed interest and a falling tax ratio, and FY2026 EPS will print below consensus. Placed high in C because the growth is all organic (against an acquisition-led past at about 6% ROIC), the EBITDA margin rises from 56% to 60%, above anything in the past, and from FY2027 EPS still compounds about 26% a year, though it rests on unguided tax, finance and FX lines.

7Scope for upgrades to guidance, sell-side estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

ConclusionOver twelve months, operating guidance is likely to be raised at most events and EBITDA estimates nudged up, but FY2026 EPS consensus faces a near-certain cut at the March 2027 results. The narrative is uncrowded but has little new to say until the cash-per-share figures of 2027 to 2028 become visible.

The dated staircase of events, with my probabilities.

Sell-side estimates: EBITDA and revenue will be nudged up, FY2026 EPS will be cut, and FY2027 to FY2028 EPS will be roughly held.

  • EBITDA and revenue estimates will rise by about 0.5 to 1.5 percent an event, cumulatively 2 to 4 percent on FY2027 by mid-2027, rather than being re-based, because the four brokers already model within 3 percent of each other and follow guidance.
  • FY2026 EPS will be cut by a quarter or more at or before March 2027, and the cut becomes mechanical once the accounts are published. On the consensus pre-tax profit, consensus net income of 99.5 USDm needs H2 2026 pre-tax profit of about 124 USDm, against about 60 USDm at the H1 run-rate of finance costs. The brokers will present the cut as "below the line" and keep their Buy ratings and their EBITDA estimates.
  • FY2027 and FY2028 EPS will be roughly held: a higher finance line (−5 to −8 percent) will be offset by putting the buyback into the share count (+4 to +6 percent), and the estimates will then drift up as the share count falls.
  • Dividend per share estimates (flat at 0.027 USD for FY2028) reflect a modelling gap and will rise.

The narrative is four brokers deep and no wider, which makes it uncrowded and fragile at once. The research found no investor voice outside the sell-side; for a FTSE 250 company trading 9 to 11 USDm of shares a day, the four brokers' notes are the whole public narrative. Most of the operating story is fully known; the timing of the growth peak and the concentration of the DRC renewals are not.

Inference and so what: the expectation gap is favourable on the lines the company reports and unfavourable on the line the model prices, and the unfavourable part arrives first. On the reported lines that the market values, guidance will be beaten, EBITDA estimates will rise and distributions will scale. On EPS, the line the model prices, consensus will fall. The favourable part also lacks novelty: under-promising and delivering is already the consensus description of the company, and it did not move the share price in July 2026. Two developments could change the narrative rather than confirm it: a refresh of the 2030 targets with a larger distribution programme (most likely by March 2028), and a disclosed DRC renewal.

Counter-case. The July 2026 experience, when beats were met by selling, may repeat. If the marginal holder is not reading the sell-side, the operating upgrades will not be rewarded until the per-share cash story is visible in the accounts, which is a 2027 to 2028 event.

What would change my view

A fifth or sixth broker initiating coverage with a cash-based framework (about 30 percent likely) would widen the narrative; a first Hold rating would narrow it. Management pre-announcing the FY2026 tax rate or finance charge at the Q3 update would defuse the March 2027 risk.

Where I differ from the market

The sell-side expects upgrades to the operating lines, and I agree. The sell-side does not expect its own FY2026 EPS cut, which I regard as near-certain. It has not put the buyback into the share count, which I regard as the cleanest upgrade to come.

Score: 56, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is likely raised or tightened up at most of the next events (60-65% each; FY2027 EBITDA guidance likely opening at 585-600 USDm and then raised), but the size is small against growth: EBITDA consensus up about 2-4% by mid-2027 against about 10% revenue growth is about 0.2-0.4 of the growth rate; the EPS line moves the wrong way first (FY2026 EPS cut by a quarter or more is near-certain, FY2027 roughly held as a higher finance line offsets the buyback), and the narrative is fully known in a 100%-Buy, four-broker story with a first Hold possible. Coherent with the fourth-set group at 52, a little higher for the guidance raises; below Teqnion, above Spie.

8Current momentum: guidance, sell-side, narrative, technicals, and the peers

ConclusionMomentum is strong and improving in guidance, operating estimates and the sell-side narrative, but the technical picture is weak (rated D), and the sector is in a down-cycle from which Helios has decoupled. The divergence between the fundamentals and the share price is both the opportunity and the warning.

Guidance momentum is strong. Guidance was raised twice in 2026, most recently in July, and the next two events (5 November and March 2027) are more likely to raise or tighten guidance than not.

Sell-side momentum is positive on EBITDA, negative on EPS and exhausted on ratings. FY2027 EBITDA and revenue consensus are up 6 percent over twelve months and 2 percent over three. FY2027 EPS consensus is down 8 percent over twelve months but up 1 percent over three and six months, so the cuts are slowing. The mean target price is up 24 percent over six months, to about 2.88 GBP (3.84 USD), 41 percent above the share price. All four brokers rate the stock a Buy, so the proportion of Buy ratings can only fall; the recent 17-point fall in that proportion reflects a contributor dropping out of the consensus. The dashboard rates sell-side earnings momentum at C and the revision score at 3.

Narrative momentum is strong on the operating story and improving on the sector's fears. Deutsche Bank's preview of 29 October ("Towering ahead") and Morgan Stanley's preview of 2 November both expect solid demand. Jefferies calls Helios its top pick in European towers. Brokers describe satellite fears as easing and the share overhang as removed.

Technical momentum is weak, and the stock is decoupled from its sector. The dashboard rates the technicals D. At 205p, the price is below the 50-day average (208.6p) and the 150-day average (208.8p), and 1.4 percent above a 200-day average that has risen in each of the last twelve months. The price is 17 percent below the May 2026 high of 247.6p, after a 21 percent jump on the Q1 update and a 23 percent give-back over the summer. Relative strength is at the 70th percentile of the universe; the share is up 36 percent over twelve months and 4 percent over six.

The stock moves on its own news and on Africa's, not with European towers. Its six-month correlation with the European tower basket is 0.27, its beta 0.48 and its R-squared 8 percent. From 13 to 23 October, Helios fell 8.2 percent while Cellnex rose 6.9 percent.

The European tower peers are in a confirmed down-cycle, and the African peers anchor private-market value at about 6x EBITDA. Cellnex carries net leverage of 6x to 7x and 2.2 EURbn of maturities in 2027; Inwit faces termination notices from its anchor tenants and a court case from November 2026; the table below gives each peer's ratings and twelve-month return. The European tower basket fell 9 percent over six months while Helios rose 4 percent. The economic peers (IHS, Indus Towers and American Tower's Africa segment) trade near 6x EBITDA, and MTN's purchase of IHS at about 6x anchors the private-market value of African towers at that level. That anchor removes the support that European towers enjoy from the expectation that a private buyer would pay more.

Inference: the fundamentals and the share price have diverged since the July beat-and-raise, and the cause is frontier-Africa sentiment and pre-IPO selling, not the European tower sector. Because the stock does not trade with the sector, the European towers' weakness does not explain the divergence. The portfolio's sector stance (towers Underweight) should therefore not be applied mechanically to this holding.

So what: the price will answer to the company's own results and to emerging-market sentiment. A stock with rising guidance, rising operating estimates, a unanimous sell-side and a D technical rating is either a stock whose marginal holder is not yet persuaded by the operating story, or a stock waiting for a specific event. Both readings point to the same catalysts: the results of 5 November and March 2027, and emerging-market sentiment. A sustained break above the 50-day and 150-day averages near 209p would be the first technical confirmation that the summer's selling has cleared.

Counter-case. A D technical rating, in a market that is shunning long-duration assets, is exactly the condition in which further delivery is ignored. The stock could trade in a 180p to 215p range through the March 2027 results and move only on the FY2027 guidance.

What would change my view

A move back above 215p on strong volume after 5 November would signal momentum turning. A break below the rising 200-day average near 202p would signal that the summer's selling has not cleared, or that frontier risk aversion is deepening.

Where I differ from the market

The market reads the stock through the sector lens (a bond proxy, rated Underweight), but the data say the sector explains only 8 percent of its variance. The relevant external factor is emerging-market and African sentiment, which no source file quantifies and the memo cannot model.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. Both measures sit above 50, but the sell-side score is essentially neutral and one part is strongly negative (three-month EPS revisions in the bottom fifth, price below its 50- and 150-day averages, 17% off its May high, D technical), so the B rule's 'none strongly negative' fails and the reading is mixed, C. Placed at the top of C because guidance was raised twice in 2026, operating estimates are rising, the narrative is improving and the price holds above a rising 200-day average; the European tower peers' down-cycle is not comparable (correlation 0.27) and is not counted.

9Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and the case

ConclusionThe operating case has one driver, is contracted and can be tracked every quarter; it is among the simplest and lowest-risk in European infrastructure. The equity case wrapped around it is not: its EPS depends on four unguided financial lines with a ±30 percent, downward-skewed range; it sits on a frontier sovereign layer with real tail risks; and it depends on a valuation multiple that matters more than all the fundamentals together.

The operating case is a one-driver story. Organic tenancy additions, generated by three operators' capex, convert into revenue at a flat 27.7k USD each and into EBITDA at about 80 percent, on a contracted base that cannot fall. The company reports the driver quarterly at a granularity few companies match: tenancies, sites and tenancy ratios by country, building-block guidance and stated rules of thumb.

The equity case is a four-driver story plus one cash line, and none of the five is guided. The four drivers are the finance charge, the tax rate, currency on intercompany loans and the share count; the cash line is capex normalisation. Each is independent of operations, two are one-sided, and all are visible only at the two annual results. The case is therefore simple to understand and simple to monitor on the lines the company reports, and hard to monitor on the line the model prices.

The five judgements that move the shares most over one to two years, with the arithmetic.

  1. Tenancy additions in FY2027 (model: 3,000). 1,000 tenancies more or fewer is about 28 USDm of annualised revenue and about 20 USDm of annualised EBITDA (10 USDm in the year itself), or 3.4 percent of FY2027 EBITDA. Depreciation barely changes (a colocation costs about 10k USD) and the finance charge does not change at all, so at an operating-company tax rate of about 30 percent, net income moves about 13 to 14 USDm: about 0.013 USD of EPS, or about 9 percent of FY2027 EPS. A fall to 2,000 additions (the low end of my range) takes FY2027 EPS from about 0.14 USD to about 0.13 USD, and FY2028 EBITDA from 649 USDm to about 629 USDm (−3 percent). I put the probability of a 1,000 miss over eighteen months at about 30 percent in each direction.
  1. Currency on intercompany loans (model: nil after H1 2026). This item is the largest single reason the FY2027 EPS range is ±30 percent and skewed down. Frontier currencies depreciate more often than they appreciate: the item was a loss of 52 USDm in FY2022 and 86 USDm in FY2023, a gain of 18 USDm in FY2025, and a loss of 22 USDm in H1 2026. The item gets no tax relief (it sits in subsidiaries with unusable losses or in holding companies), so it falls straight to net income. A 30 USDm loss in FY2027 would cut net income from 142 USDm to 112 USDm (−21 percent) and EPS from 0.14 USD to about 0.11 USD; a repeat of the 86 USDm loss would cut EPS by more than half. In my judgement, the expected value is a loss of about 10 to 15 USDm a year (about 7 to 10 percent of FY2027 EPS), and a loss of 20 to 40 USDm is about 25 percent likely in any given year.
  1. The tax rate (model: 37.8 percent in FY2027, including minorities). Five points on FY2027 pre-tax profit of 228 USDm is about 11 USDm, or about 8 percent of net income. A 10-point swing in a single year is within recent experience (about 16 percent of EPS): the FY2025 charge contained a 64 USDm unwind of deferred tax assets, and the FY2026 interim rate was struck at 45.6 percent. The downward trend in the rate is mechanical, because a charge fixed in dollars is spread over a fast-growing pre-tax profit, but the level in any one year is noisy. Separately, about 104 to 106 USDm of unprovided tax assessments could cost a one-off 10 to 30 USDm of cash over four years.
  1. The DRC renewals in 2028 to 2029 (model: a concession of about 1 percent of group revenue). The renewing Airtel Africa and Orange contracts in the DRC carry of the order of 250 USDm of annual revenue. A 15 percent price cut on those contracts would remove about 37 USDm of revenue and the same amount of EBITDA, because with indexation-only pricing the whole cut falls on margin: about 3 percent of FY2029 revenue and 5 percent of FY2029 EBITDA. After about 30 percent operating-company tax, the cut is about 26 USDm of net income, or 13 percent of FY2029 EPS (0.22 USD to about 0.19 USD). A clean renewal would add back the 11 USDm the model already deducts (+4 percent of FY2029 EPS). Over three years, I put the probability of a material concession at about 25 to 30 percent, of a clean renewal at 15 to 20 percent, and of the most likely outcome, a modest escalator cap or freeze traded for ten more years, at 50 to 60 percent.
  1. The multiple (model: 26.28x two-year-forward P/E; today 16.7x). The multiple is the largest number in the return and the one least connected to the business; it is worth more than judgements 1 to 4 combined, in both directions. Each turn of EV/EBITDA on FY2027 EBITDA of 598 USDm is about 21 percent of the market value; each 1x of P/E on two-year-forward EPS of about 0.16 USD is about 6 percent of the share price. The model's return to December 2027 is +117 percent at 26.28x, about +65 percent at 20x and about +39 percent at an unchanged 16.7x; the trough cases in section 11 are −12 to −29 percent, at 7.0x to 6.5x forward EBITDA.

A sixth, smaller lever is the share count. 100 USDm of buyback at 2.75 USD a share retires about 36m shares, 3.6 percent of the count and therefore 3.6 percent of EPS; at 3.70 USD a share it retires 27m. The model's 99 USDm of buybacks in FY2027 is announced and funded; the 110 to 180 USDm a year afterwards is a policy assumption worth about 4 to 7 percent of EPS a year.

Sudden, material and hard-to-track risks: each is unlikely on its own, but the joint probability that none occurs within eighteen months is low. Most would hit reported EPS and the multiple; two (a restriction on repatriating cash and a repricing at renewal) would hit the case itself. The table gives my probability and the magnitude of each.

  • The DRC rule banning physical foreign-currency cash from 9 April 2027 is the dated precursor of a repatriation restriction, and it is probably benign because collections are electronic and billed in dollars.
  • Axian is the most exposed of the top five customers to a credit event or dispute; the company already leaves 46.8 USDm of potential contract revenue unrecognised.
  • A devaluation or default would be small on EBITDA, because 71 percent of EBITDA is in hard or pegged currencies, but large on reported EPS through the currency item in judgement 2.

Over eighteen months, perception risks are more probable than fundamental ones. The main perception risks are: a sequential fall in additions read as a slowdown (on 5 November, then every quarter); the FY2026 EPS miss (March 2027); interest rates and the bond-proxy trade; a Nigerian or Ghanaian currency event read across to Helios; the Inwit trial reopening the question of whether tower master service agreements are sacrosanct; SpaceX headlines; the first non-Buy rating; and a thin bench of analysts (three or four brokers, with one handover already in 2026).

Sector precedents: towers outperform when three conditions coincide, and Helios has two of them. The three are lease-up on a fixed base, deleveraging with buybacks, and a stable or falling cost of capital; Helios lacks the third. Towers underperform on rising rates (Cellnex fell from 60 to 30 EUR), customer consolidation or churn (American Tower's US growth slowed to about 1 percent; Inwit's termination notices; MasOrange removing 1,500 sites from Cellnex), emerging-market customer distress (American Tower's reserves against Vodafone Idea and its exit from India), currency collapse (IHS and the naira) and leveraged acquisitions (Helios's own 45 percent fall in 2023 at 5.1x leverage). Helios carries the emerging-market credit and currency triggers at lower intensity than IHS did (71 percent of EBITDA in hard currency, against 38 percent at IHS), and it has retired the acquisition trigger.

What would change my view

Any of the dated events in section 7 landing outside the thresholds stated there; a currency loss above 40 USDm in a half-year; disclosure of the DRC renewal terms.

Where I differ from the market

The sell-side treats the case as low-risk because the operating lines are low-risk; it has not priced the EPS range or the DRC concentration. The market, through the share price, treats Helios as a frontier risk asset at 8.5x EBITDA. Both are right about the line each is looking at; my point is that they are describing different lines.

Score: 41, set by the Rater. The operating case is one trackable driver on a contracted base (FY2027 EBITDA cone about +/-4%), but the share price rests on EPS with a +/-30%, downward-skewed FY2027 cone driven by four unguided lines (FX on intercompany loans, tax, finance, share count), on 3.4-3.8x leverage, a frontier sovereign layer with sudden tails (repatriation 5-10%, devaluations 15-20%), 72% customer concentration and a multiple worth more than all fundamentals together (trough -12% to -29%). Between the 36 and 54 Risks groups; a little below OMV Petrom's sudden fiscal risk, a little above Fevertree.

10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

ConclusionHelios is turning up on the earnings line and already reinforcing on the operating line. The thesis is due to broaden into cash-per-share compounding through 2027 and 2028, but the share faces a real risk of looking stalled during the 2027 deceleration and the March 2027 EPS print.

The dashboard places the stock at Turning/Inflecting, but the business, the earnings and the share price are at three different points.

  • The operating company is reinforcing: ten years of EBITDA growth, fourteen quarterly beats, two guidance raises this year, record additions, distributions started and credit ratings upgraded.
  • The earnings line is turning up from nothing: reported EPS of 0.037 USD in FY2025, about 0.07 USD in FY2026 and about 0.14 USD in FY2027, the first years in which the P/E is a meaningful number.
  • The share price is stalling: 17 percent below its May high, below its 50-day and 150-day averages, after a failed response to the July beat-and-raise; the two-year-forward P/E has round-tripped from 7.4x (December 2024) to 22.6x (May 2026) and back to 18.6x.

Inference: the first leg of the re-rating is done, and the second leg needs cash per share to show in the accounts. The first leg (the P/E rising from about 7x to 20x, and the share price up about 80 percent in the twelve months to spring 2026) was the market recognising that the company would make a profit and return cash. The second leg requires the thesis to broaden from "EBITDA grows" to "cash per share compounds". That broadening needs the buyback to show in the share count, the dividend to be paid from cash upstreamed by the operating companies, and leverage to fall through 3.0x: all events of 2027.

Between the two legs sits the configuration in which a stock looks stalled even while its thesis is intact. In that interval, the growth rate visibly decelerates (additions from Q3 2026, revenue from H2 2027) and the EPS line prints below consensus (March 2027).

So what: the most plausible path is turning up through March 2027, then broadening through H2 2027 and 2028, with a stall risk in H2 2027. The scope for upgrades (operating lines, share count, 2030 targets) points to turning up and broadening. The momentum (a D technical rating and negative EPS revisions) points to stalling. The risk factors (frontier exposure and the wide EPS range) cap the phase at turning rather than reinforcing. The stall risk is that the market reads the deceleration as the end of the growth story before it has started to pay for the cash story.

Counter-case. If the operator cycle is prolonged (Jefferies's reading), the deceleration does not arrive in 2027 and the stock moves straight from turning up to reinforcing; if emerging-market sentiment turns, the multiple does the work regardless. Conversely, a currency shock or a DRC event in 2027 would make "collapsing" the right word for the share, though not for the business.

What would change my view

A rise through the May 2026 high of 247.6p on the March 2027 guidance would mark the broadening leg as under way. A break of the 200-day average after a clean operating print would mark a stall.

Where I differ from the market

The dashboard and I agree on Turning/Inflecting. The sell-side's narrative is already at "reinforcing" (a top pick and a compounding platform), while the price is at "stalling". In my view, the stock earns "reinforcing" only once the per-share cash figures are in the accounts, a 2027 to 2028 event, and the 2027 deceleration is the test of whether it gets there.

Score: 58, set by the Rater. The computed Turning/Inflecting is right for the earnings line (EPS turning up from 0.037 USD) but the operating line is in a well-known Reinforcing phase (fourteen beats, all-Buy coverage, conservatism the consensus description) and the next six to twelve months bring a sequential fall in additions, an FY2026 EPS miss and the growth peak in H1 2027, while the price is stalling (D technical, failed response to the July raise); broadening into cash per share is a 2027-28 event. Below Nexans's paused Reinforcing, above Greggs's Bottoming.

11The fair multiple

ConclusionThe guideline fair multiple of 26.28x is a ceiling drawn from a history that carries little information, not a central case for the next eighteen months. My fair multiple is about 20x two-year-forward earnings (about 9.5x forward EBITDA), with a trough of 13x to 14x (6.5x to 7.0x EBITDA). The return in section 12 should be read against all three.

The guideline is 26.28x two-year-forward earnings. Viewforth's guideline for a Turning/Inflecting stock is the 60th percentile of the stock's own ten-year history of that multiple (71 months), here 26.28x, which is 42 percent above today's 18.55x on FactSet (16.7x in the model at 2.05 GBP). The model reaches the guideline multiple at its December 2027 column.

The ten-year history is a poor anchor, because for most of it the company lost money or barely broke even. Two-year-forward P/Es were 93x to 105x at the 2019 IPO, 36x to 180x in 2020 to 2021 and 60x to 176x in 2022 to 2023. The P/E then fell to 7.4x in December 2024, as earnings turned positive with the price at 91p, and rose to 22.6x in May 2026 with the price at 235p. The ten-year percentiles (10th 7.2x, median 21.2x, 75th 37.5x) therefore describe the arithmetic of small denominators, not any view the market held about the company. The P/E has carried information only in the last two years (median 14.3x, range 7.4x to 22.6x), and today's 18.6x sits in the upper half of that range.

The market actually values Helios on EV/EBITDA and free cash flow yield, and on those measures the guideline implies a multiple no African tower asset has ever commanded.

  • Today: 8.5x FY2026 EBITDA and 7.5x FY2027 EBITDA; a recurring free cash flow yield of about 9 percent on 2027 (Jefferies).
  • Reference points: about 6x for IHS and Indus Towers, and the price MTN is paying for IHS; 14x to 16x historically for Cellnex and Inwit, a level Helios has never approached because of the frontier discount.
  • Brokers' targets: a mean of about 2.88 GBP (41 percent above the price) implies about 8.8x FY2028 EBITDA, roughly today's multiple rolled forward a year.
  • The guideline: 26.28x FY2029 EPS at December 2027 implies a price of about 4.46 GBP and an equity value of about 5.7 USDbn. With about 2.0 USDbn of net debt, that equity value is about 11.8x FY2028 EBITDA and 11.1x FY2029 EBITDA. Reaching it would require the frontier discount to close toward European levels.

My view: a fair two-year-forward P/E of about 20x, because three arguments pull in different directions and 20x balances them.

  1. The lifecycle phase argues for a multiple below the stock's own peak-delivery level, because forecasts of the valued line (EPS) are uncertain and the growth rate is about to decelerate visibly.
  2. The record argues for a premium to IHS and Indus Towers (6x EBITDA), because Helios leases up at twice their rate and has retired its leverage and acquisition risks.
  3. The EPS growth path (+100 percent, +28 percent, +23 percent) argues that a P/E in the high teens or low twenties on two-year-forward earnings is undemanding against that growth.

At the December 2027 column, 20x is about 9.5x forward EBITDA. That multiple sits inside the 6.5x to 9.5x range I would defend for the stock through this phase, and roughly at the top of the meaningful two-year P/E range. I regard the guideline's 26.28x as the multiple the stock could reach if emerging-market sentiment turned and the per-share cash story were fully visible (a 2028 outcome at best), not as a central case for December 2027. The trough is 6.5x to 7.0x forward EBITDA (about 13x to 14x P/E), between the private-market reference and today's multiple, giving 145p to 180p.

Counter-case. The guideline's logic is that a Turning/Inflecting stock reverts toward its own median as delivery proves out, and Helios's EPS range will narrow sharply once FY2027 is reported. If the market then capitalises 20 percent EPS growth at a growth multiple, 26x two-year-forward earnings is not extravagant: it is about 1.2 times the EPS growth rate. The stock's decoupling from European towers also means its multiple is set by its own results rather than by a de-rating sector.

What would change my view

A fall in US yields or an emerging-market rally would move the multiple toward the guideline without any change in the business. A DRC renewal disclosed on clean terms would move my fair multiple toward 22x to 24x. A currency or repatriation event would move it toward the trough.

Where I differ from the market and the guideline

The market applies about 8.5x EBITDA and has not moved that multiple in a year, despite two guidance raises. The guideline applies 26.28x earnings, on a history generated by what was effectively a different company. I sit between them: a multiple that holds roughly where it is in P/E terms while earnings double, which still delivers most of the return.

Score: 66, set by the Rater. Neutral on both gives C. Placed in the upper half because the peer reading is all but cheap and the memo's fair 20x two-year-forward P/E sits above today's 18.6x; held off the top because the ten-year range is a loss-making company's small-denominator history and part of the discount is deserved (frontier sovereign layer, private-market reference near 6x EBITDA against 8.5x today, a visible deceleration ahead).

12Total shareholder return

ConclusionThe earnings leg of the return (+37 percent to December 2027, +84 percent to June 2029) is well founded in contracted volume, fixed interest, a falling tax ratio and a shrinking share count. The multiple leg (+57 percent at the guideline) is an option on emerging-market sentiment, not a forecast. My central return is about +65 percent to December 2027 and about +120 percent to June 2029, and about +39 percent and +86 percent at an unchanged multiple.

The return of record, at the guideline fair multiple. The model starts from 2.05 GBP on 28 October 2026 and a two-year-forward P/E of 16.7x, with the multiple rising to 26.28x by the December 2027 column.

The earnings part is the growth in two-year-forward EPS, from about 0.163 USD today to about 0.22 USD at December 2027 (FY2029 EPS) and about 0.30 USD at June 2029.

What drives the earnings part: EBITDA supplies about a third, and the three leverage effects and the buyback supply two thirds. On the model's FY2027 to FY2029 path (the cleanest two-year window, because FY2026 is distorted by the currency loss and the interim tax rate), EPS rises 55 percent, about 24 percent a year. The five factors set out in section 5 have specific sources: EBITDA (+16 percent) comes from average tenancies up 9.5 and 7.2 percent and the margin up 1.7 points; operating leverage (+3 percent) from depreciation growing only 4 to 5 percent a year; financial leverage (+14 percent) from a flat 180 USDm finance charge against operating profit up 19 percent; the tax ratio (+6 percent) from a dollar charge on a faster-growing pre-tax profit; and the share count (+7 percent) from buybacks of 99 and 110 USDm.

The rest of the earnings contribution in the 18-month column comes from FY2026 to FY2027, when EPS rises 102 percent. That rise reflects the full-year carry of 2026's additions, the absence in FY2027 of the 21.8 USDm currency loss and of the high interim tax rate, and the redemption of the convertible bond.

The multiple part depends entirely on the assumption in section 11. The split makes the dependence explicit: the multiple supplies 57 of the 117 points to December 2027 at the guideline, about 20 points at my 20x, and nothing at an unchanged multiple.

The unchanged-multiple case (+39 percent, 2.81 GBP) coincides with the brokers' mean target, which is what one would expect from brokers who roll today's EV/EBITDA multiple forward a year.

Dividends are small in the return (1.6 to 2.8 percent), but cash returns are large in the mechanism. The dividend is 25 USDm, growing over 10 percent a year (a yield of about 1.2 percent). The 175 USDm buyback to December 2027 and the assumed 110 to 180 USDm a year afterwards return about 5 to 6 percent of market value a year, and that return shows up in the earnings part, through the share count, rather than in the dividend line. On the model's assumptions, total cash returned from FY2026 to FY2030 is about 745 USDm, about a quarter of today's market value.

25 USDmFY2026 dividend, growing over 10% a year (about 1.2% yield)
175 USDmbuyback to December 2027
110 to 180 USDma year of buybacks assumed afterwards
about 745 USDmreturned FY2026 to FY2030: about a quarter of today's market value

The return is fragile where it is struck and robust where it is earned. It is fragile because it is struck on EPS at a P/E multiple, so it inherits the ±30 percent EPS range and the one-sided currency and tax items; a 30 USDm currency loss in FY2027 would take about 20 percent off the earnings part. It is robust because the EBITDA and cash paths behind it have a ±4 percent range, the 2027 share count is funded and announced, and an unchanged multiple still delivers +39 percent and +86 percent. The return is therefore better described as "+40 to +65 percent to December 2027 from earnings and buybacks, with the multiple as an option" than as the model's +117 percent.

Counter-case. The three-year return at the guideline (+192 percent) is a plausible outcome if the DRC renewals are traded cleanly, emerging-market sentiment turns and distributions step up toward the 800 USDm that Deutsche Bank thinks the company can return. I attach a probability of about 20 percent to all three happening by mid-2029.

What would change my view

The multiple triggers in section 11; a currency or tax event in FY2027; FY2027 opening EBITDA guidance above 600 USDm, which would make me lift the earnings part.

Where I differ from the market

The market's implied return (the brokers' targets) is about +40 percent on an unchanged EBITDA multiple, which matches my unchanged-multiple case almost exactly. The model's +117 percent needs a re-rating that no African tower asset has had. My central case sits between the two.
